item.title: Chinese naval vessels, tanks arrive in Ream as China-Cambodia 'Golden Dragon-2026' exercise preparations advance
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-24 21:25:00
Three PLA Navy vessels, the Type 071 amphibious landing ship Kunlunshan (Hull 998), the Type 054A guided-missile frigate Xuchang (Hull 536) and the Type 903A comprehensive replenishment ship Wulunguhu (Hull 893), dock at the Cambodia-China Joint Support and Training Center at Port Ream, Cambodia. Photo: PLA Southern Theater Command Preparations for the "Golden Dragon 2026" joint exercise between the Chinese and Cambodian militaries are progressing steadily at the Cambodia-China Joint Support and Training Center at Port Ream, the PLA Southern Theater Command said on Tuesday, releasing photos that showed several naval vessels and main battle tanks arriving at the center. The Chinese and Cambodian militaries will hold the 8th "Golden Dragon-2026" joint exercise in Cambodia from late November to mid-December, focusing on counterterrorism, anti-piracy and humanitarian rescue operations, China's Ministry of National Defense announced on Tuesday. Preparations have been proceeding smoothly since Chinese troops arrived at the Cambodia-China Joint Support and Training Center in Ream on November 22, with Chinese and Cambodian forces working in close coordination, the Southern Theater Command said. The photos showed three Chinese naval vessels at the Port Ream center: the Kunlunshan (Hull 998), a Type 071 amphibious landing ship; the Xuchang (Hull 536), a Type 054A guided-missile frigate; and the Wulunguhu (Hull 893), a Type 903A comprehensive replenishment ship. The images also showed Type 96 main battle tanks carried aboard the Kunlunshan disembarking. Type 96 main battle tanks disembarks from the Kunlunshan. Photo: PLA Southern Theater Command The exercise is scheduled to include familiarization training, command-post exercises and comprehensive live-force drills. After arriving in Cambodia, Chinese participating forces from the PLA Army, Navy, Air Force and Joint Logistics Support Force quickly moved by road to their designated deployment areas, while Chinese and Cambodian command elements stepped up preparations - coordinating operational plans, conducting site inspections and carrying out joint communications tests, according to the Southern Theater Command. The exercise will play a positive role in the building of an all-weather China-Cambodia community with a shared future in the new era, China's Ministry of National Defense said. The Cambodia-China Joint Support and Training Center was officially put into operation on April 5, 2025, according to the Xinhua News Agency. At the inauguration ceremony, both sides emphasized that the center was built and operates on the basis of mutual respect and equal consultation between China and Cambodia, which helps strengthening the practical cooperation, better fulfill international obligations and provide international public security goods. Alongside the ceremony, the Chinese and Cambodian militaries launched the "Golden Dragon 2025" joint exercise at the center, with vessels of both sides conducting in formation maneuvers, maritime communications, and equipment exercises. item.title: Alibaba rejects US blacklisting of Singapore subsidiary as widening chip curbs threaten regional AI cooperation
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-24 21:19:00
Concept picture of AI Photo: VCG Chinese tech giant Alibaba has rejected as erroneous US decision to add its Singapore subsidiary to the Entity List, vowing to pursue all legal avenues to protect its legitimate rights and reputation, as Washington increasingly extends its chip export controls to overseas business networks on the grounds of potential security risks. The expanding restrictions, based on presumed risks rather than proven violations, could disrupt normal commercial activities and undermine AI investment and industrial cooperation across Southeast Asia, a Chinese industry analyst said on Tuesday. The US Department of Commerce moved on Monday to blacklist Alibaba's Singapore-based subsidiary Apex Enterprise Solutions alongside six other Southeast Asian entities, including Megaspeed International, a cloud computing company under US investigation over suspected circumvention of chip export controls, Reuters and Bloomberg reported. The Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) cited a significant risk that the seven entities were or could become involved in diverting advanced computing products to unauthorized users or uses. But the rule did not detail any specific violations by Apex. "Adding Apex Enterprise Solutions to the Entity List is erroneous because Apex has never diverted advanced computing chips subject to US export restrictions. We will seek all legal avenues to protect our rights and reputation," Alibaba told the Global Times on Tuesday. Alibaba challenged its inclusion on the Pentagon's 1260H list of companies allegedly supporting the Chinese military in June. The company secured an initial legal victory in late October, when a US federal judge ruled in its favor and blocked certain Pentagon restrictions, Reuters reported on October 27. Besides Apex and Megaspeed International, the latest rule lists MSFusion, PT Megaspeed International and Speedmatrix under Malaysia, Swiftdata under Singapore, and Megaspeed (Thailand) under Thailand, according to the BIS document. Several of the newly listed companies had previously defended the legitimacy or independence of their business operations. MSFusion denied having any equity links with Megaspeed International in a November 16 statement on its website, stressing that its operations, management and decision-making were free from any direct or indirect external control, Malaysian newspaper The Star reported on Tuesday. Megaspeed said in a statement on its website on November 12 that it took its compliance obligations under US export control laws "extremely seriously" and had retained a US law firm to independently verify its export control compliance practices. The latest listings signal a broader shift in US export control policy, Ma Jihua, a veteran industry analyst, told the Global Times on Tuesday. "As China's AI capabilities advance, Washington is continually 'patching' its control regime to target overseas subsidiaries, business partners and affiliated entities." US restrictions are increasingly based on presumed risks rather than proven violations. Companies could find themselves subject to restrictions simply for being part of a particular supply chain or business network, Ma said, adding that this exposes businesses to growing compliance risks and makes it increasingly difficult to determine what constitutes permissible commercial activity. The latest blacklisting coincided with Nvidia's announcement on Monday that Jensen Huang had been reinstated as president and CEO, with its board saying his return "poses no national security risk." Nvidia shares surged more than 31 percent, adding about $1 trillion to its market value. Huang's reinstatement followed weeks of intense US media coverage of espionage allegations involving a former Megaspeed executive and mounting political scrutiny of the chipmaker. Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun dismissed the "Chinese spy" allegation as "purely unsubstantiated and directed at smearing China." Greater US scrutiny will force companies to reassess the compliance risks of overseas subsidiaries, suppliers and partners, complicating operations and weighing on investment decisions, Ma noted. Over time, the restrictions could accelerate Chinese investment in domestically developed chips and computing infrastructure, he added. The economic repercussions extend well beyond Chinese companies. Banks and private credit funds financing Southeast Asian data centers and AI chip purchases face the risk of losing key Chinese customers, with tighter US chip controls prompting lenders to reassess planned financing deals, Bloomberg reported. The Semiconductor Industry Association has said that excessive export controls could cost American chipmakers key markets and weaken their competitiveness. Overseas customers accounted for more than 70 percent of their revenue in 2025, according to the association. By restricting access to these markets, Washington risks undermining the very technological edge it seeks to protect. Ma warned that mounting operational and financing pressures could slow Southeast Asia's digital transformation. Yet the region's commercial interest in the Chinese market could drive it toward more independent technology partnerships, potentially fragmenting global computing markets and raising costs. "From chips and computing power to large AI models, successive rounds of US restrictions have failed to halt China's technological progress. The effectiveness of administrative measures is limited in the face of strong market forces, and such restrictions could ultimately prove counterproductive," Ma said.

item.title: China urges EU to uphold non-discrimination principle in provisional safeguard measures on hybrid vehicle imports
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-24 19:40:00
The Ministry of Commerce of China File photo: VCG China on Tuesday urged the EU to honor bilateral consensus, strictly abide by World Trade Organization (WTO) rules and uphold the principle of non-discrimination in its safeguard investigation into imported hybrid vehicles, vowing to safeguard the legitimate rights and interests of Chinese industries. The remarks came after the European Commission on Tuesday released its preliminary findings in a global safeguard investigation into imported hybrid vehicles, with provisional safeguard measures set to take effect on December 1. The EU launched the safeguard investigation on October 30 and decided to impose provisional measures less than a month later, China's Ministry of Commerce (MOFCOM) said in response to a media inquiry. Prior to the launch of the investigation, China and the EU had held consultations under their trade and investment consultation mechanism, based on the principles of mutual respect and consultation on an equal footing, reaching a lawful, pragmatic and balanced arrangement on hybrid vehicle trade, MOFCOM said. China will closely monitor subsequent developments in the EU investigation and reserves all rights, including resorting to dispute settlement and seeking trade compensation under the WTO framework, to firmly safeguard the legitimate rights and interests of relevant Chinese industries, MOFCOM noted. The ministry reiterated that protectionism leads nowhere and that openness and cooperation are the right way forward. At a critical stage in the green transition of the global automotive industry, openness and cooperation are an inevitable trend. The Chinese and European automotive industries have complementary strengths and are deeply integrated, and closer cooperation serves the common interests of both sides, MOFCOM said. China hopes the EU will work in the same direction as China to provide a stable, predictable and sustainable trade and investment environment for industries on both sides, while promoting the stable, balanced and healthy development of bilateral economic and trade relations, the ministry said. Global Times

item.title: Chinese ministry employee sentenced to death over espionage for foreign spy agency
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-24 17:21:00
Photo: Screenshot from Baomiguan An employee in an unspecified Chinese ministry who was once stationed overseas has been sentenced to death for espionage after providing more than 100 pieces of confidential information collected through his work to a foreign intelligence agency in exchange for over 1 million yuan in payments. Baomiguan, a WeChat public account linked to China's National Administration of State Secrets Protection, disclosed the case in an article on Monday. While stationed in an unnamed country, the ministry employee surnamed Ma was approached by an intelligence officer named Kailin from another country, who initially used language learning and communication as pretexts before probing into politically sensitive issues and the personnel and operations of the Chinese institution in country where Ma is stationed. Ma disclosed a substantial amount of sensitive information about the Chinese institution to Kailin and provided her with an internal telephone directory. Kailin later introduced him to her colleague named Tang Zheng, who demanded that Ma join the intelligence agency with Kailin and threatened to expose his past illegal activities to Chinese authorities if he refuses. Ma accepted espionage assignments from the intelligence agency of country of Kailin, signed a "cooperation agreement" that included clauses of "confidentiality" and "loyalty," and regularly received a fixed monthly payment. Tang also supplied Ma with a laptop to transmit and receive intelligence. After completing his overseas assignment and returning to China, Ma spent an extended period stealing classified information from documents and materials accessed through his work and transmitting the information to the foreign country via an espionage website. He provided more than 100 pieces of intelligence in exchange for payments and performance-based bonuses and collected the payments through meetings held either in China or overseas. Ma was eventually apprehended. The court found that Ma provided state secrets to a foreign intelligence agency over an extended period, with nine items classified as top secret and 26 classified as secret. In return, Ma received more than 1 million yuan ($150,143) in espionage payments. The court sentenced Ma to death for espionage, deprived him of his political rights for life, and ordered the confiscation of all his personal property. The article warned that foreign espionage and intelligence agencies are increasingly using sophisticated and deceptive tactics such as emotional manipulation, financial incentives, threats and blackmail to target personnel in key positions at government bodies, stressing that such cases offer serious lessons. item.title: Exhibition highlights contributions of international friends in wartime China
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-24 13:04:00
A man visits an exhibition at the Museum of the Communist Party of China in Beijing, capital of China, Nov. 23, 2026. The exhibition titled "Great Bridge Builders Edgar Snow and International Friends in Yan'an" was opened here on Monday. Featuring the individual stories and collective memories of 216 international friends, the exhibition traces a historical journey from wartime support to enduring friendship. (Xinhua/Jin Liangkuai) An exhibition was launched in the Museum of the Communist Party of China (CPC) in Beijing on Monday highlighting the contributions of international friends, including American journalist Edgar Snow, during China's wartime years and paying tribute to friendships that transcended national borders. Titled "Great Bridge Builders: Edgar Snow and International Friends in Yan'an", the exhibition features 150 cultural relics and archival documents, 402 photographs, and seven documentaries. It tells the stories of international friends who broke through multiple blockades to reach Yan'an, China's revolutionary heartland, about 90 years ago, supported the Chinese revolution, and helped build a bridge of dialogue between the CPC, the Chinese people, and the world. This year marks the 90th anniversary of the victory of the Long March by the Red Army under the leadership of the CPC, and also the 90th anniversary of Snow's first visit to the revolutionary base in northern Shaanxi, which inspired his renowned work "Red Star Over China." His works helped introduce the Chinese revolution in the 1930s to the world and inspired many other international people to visit Yan'an. The exhibition is co-hosted by the publicity department of the CPC Shaanxi provincial committee, the Museum of the CPC and the CPC Yan'an municipal committee, and organized by the Yan'an Revolutionary Memorial Hall. Highlights include a 1938 Chinese edition of Red Star Over China published in Shanghai, and an inscribed copy of Helen Snow's Inside Red China. Liu Ni, director of the Yan'an Revolutionary Memorial Hall, said that more items are being donated. For instance, Sharon Crain, a friend of Edgar Snow's wife Helen, donated two suitcases the couple once used. The suitcases are currently on the way to China. Visitors can also find items such as a camera used by American doctor George Hatem in Yan'an, a replica of German doctor Hans Muller's wallet, and documents from American experts Erwin Engst and Joan Hinton. "As descendants visiting this exhibition, viewing these artifacts and archival photos, we gain a deeper appreciation for the simple yet profound friendship our ancestors forged when they chose to put down roots in this land," said Dehua Muller, son of Hans. "We are committed to passing this friendship on." Fred Engst, son of Erwin Engst and Joan Hinton, observed that while official diplomacy serves as a "big bridge" between nations, people-to-people exchanges form the "small bridges." He explained: "The big bridge bears the critical mission of connecting countries, while the smaller bridges link the hearts of ordinary people. Only when both converge can mutual understanding truly endure." The exhibition will last for three months in Beijing. item.title: What is China's takeaway from Jensen Huang's saga?
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-24 12:42:00
Jensen Huang. Photo: VCG Eleven days ago, almost no one would have imagined Jensen Huang walking away from Nvidia. Eleven days later, he was back - in a way few could have predicted - reclaiming his place at the very center of the company's power structure. In the space of just eleven days, certain American media outlets and politicians turned the episode into a Hollywood-style spectacle, complete with gossip, conspiracy theories, and political maneuvering. And then? Huang is back, "posing no national security risk." "Is it a threat to have him? No, it's a threat to lose him," the US President said, defending the return. Some Western media outlets spent weeks digging up dirt on him, branding him a "spy," and portraying him as a deeply troubled figure — both personally and professionally. They may be having a hard time explaining what happened next. There he was: Jensen Huang, strolling back into Nvidia headquarters in a dark blue jacket, greeted by cheering employees, a forest of raised phones, and thunderous applause. The Financial Times struck a sour note, casting Huang's return as "a triumph of money over morals." But is that really what happened? Huang's fate was never simply a matter of personal conduct. His future became a pawn in a much bigger game - one involving elections, political infighting, semiconductors, and geopolitics. He made his way back because, after all the political maneuvering and calculations, one thing became clear: The so-called spy allegations, entirely fabricated out of thin air, are nothing more than a political witch hunt; Nvidia and US AI industry still need him. While certain politicians in Washington scramble to carve up the AI compute pie, Silicon Valley's engineers have sent a very different message through their applause: Politics may create enemies, but technological competition is ultimately won through real-world capabilities. You don't win the AI race through political witch hunts or a never-ending expansion of export controls. You win by keeping the people who know how to build, innovate, and deliver. Those invoking "national security" may have plenty to say about GPUs. But the people who actually design and build them know what it takes to stay ahead in the AI race. The Huang episode has also given global markets a fresh and sobering perspective on the relationship between business and government in the US, the country's business climate, and how corporate power really works. In America, the fate of tech companies is never determined by market forces and technological prowess alone. It is deeply intertwined with politics, making even the biggest companies vulnerable to partisan battles, geopolitical rivalries, and political maneuvering. Even for a company as powerful as Nvidia, who really gets to decide something as basic as whether the CEO stays or leaves? After this episode, companies and investors around the world may need to rethink what they thought they knew about doing business in the US, how corporations and government interact, and what corporate independence actually means. Huang is back, but the storm is far from over. More hearings and investigations are on the way and the winds of McCarthyism are still blowing. This farce has shown just how unpredictable and politicized the US business environment has become, and it has given China a clear reminder. Every restriction, political intervention, and so-called national security review Washington has imposed on China's tech industry only reinforces the same lesson: China has no choice but to accelerate its drive for technological self-reliance and build a fully integrated, independent semiconductor supply chain. What is China's takeaway from Jensen Huang's saga? A clearer view of the absurd relationship between American politics and technology - or, more simply, another episode of the American political soap opera.

item.title: MPS unveils 10 cases of AI-generated online rumors as part of crackdown on rumor-related offenses
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-24 11:35:00
Photo: Screenshot from Sina Weibo The cybersecurity bureau of China's Ministry of Public Security (MPS) on Tuesday released 10 typical cases involving the fabrication and spread of AI-generated online rumors in 2026, as part of ongoing efforts to crack down on rumor-related offenses under the "Clean Internet 2026" campaign. In one case, an internet user surnamed Ma used AI tools to fabricate a video of the glass-bottom bridge at Zhangjiajie Grand Canyon in Central China's Hunan Province collapsing to attract attention and traffic. Falsely showing the bridge breaking apart and people fleeing in panic, the video carried the caption "There's no need to go out for fun unless you have to. It's safer to stay at home." The video sparked public panic and disrupted public order. Local police have since taken criminal compulsory measures against Ma in accordance with the law. In another case, an internet user surnamed Han used AI tools to create and post fake images and videos of himself in a police uniform against a backdrop of police insignia and vehicles to attract attention and traffic. The content misled users, disrupted public order, and had a negative social impact, and local police have since taken criminal compulsory measures against Han in accordance with the law. A netizen surnamed Shu used AI tools to generate a fake video of a production line for toxic, artificially produced rice in Central China's Hubei Province to attract attention. The video spread fabricated food-safety rumors, causing public panic and disrupting public order. Local police have imposed administrative penalties on Shu. Another case involved an internet user surnamed Sun who used AI tools to fabricate false information about a case in which authorities had seized smuggled rare earths worth 4.6 billion yuan ($690 million) in Lianyungang, East China's Jiangsu Province. Local police have imposed administrative penalties on Sun in accordance with the law. An internet user surnamed Wang used AI to fabricate screenshots of social media posts impersonating an entertainer in an attempt to express personal dissatisfaction. The fake posts, written in the entertainer's voice, expressed discontent and falsely claimed that a performance had been called off. The content had a negative impact and disrupted public order. Local police have imposed administrative penalties on Wang. In another case, a netizen surnamed Xing used AI to use a public figure's likeness in livestream sales on an online platform without authorization. The unauthorized use misled internet viewers and caused serious adverse impacts. Local police have imposed administrative penalties on Xing. The MPS reminded the public that deliberately fabricating or spreading rumors, or falsely reporting emergencies, epidemics, disasters, or police incidents can result in up to 10 days of detention and a fine of up to 1,000 yuan for minor offenses - or up to seven years in prison for serious ones. item.title: Shenzhou-24 crew unveiled; first foreign astronaut joins China's space mission
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-24 09:51:00
China Manned Space Agency (CMSA) on November 24, 2026, unveiled the Shenzhou-24 crew: spacecraft pilot Tang Hongbo (center), flight engineer Wu Yi (right), and payload specialist Muhammad Zeeshan Ali (left). The China Manned Space Agency (CMSA) on Tuesday unveiled the Shenzhou-24 crew: spacecraft pilot Tang Hongbo, flight engineer Wu Yi, and payload specialist Muhammad Zeeshan Ali. Tang will serve as the mission commander. This marks the first crew in China's manned space programs to include a foreign astronaut. Commander Tang previously flew on the Shenzhou 12 and Shenzhou 17 missions and is set to become the first Chinese astronaut to visit the Tiangong space station three times. Wu Yi is a member of the third cohort of Chinese astronauts. Muhammad Zeeshan Ali is among the first foreign astronauts selected under the cooperation agreement between China and Pakistan. Both Wu Yi and Muhammad Zeeshan Ali will be making their maiden spaceflight, according to CMSA. Under the mission plan, after a short duration stay aboard the space station, the first foreign astronaut will return to Earth aboard the Shenzhou-23 spacecraft. Zhu Yangzhu, a member of the Shenzhou-23 crew, will remain in orbit to take part in the Shenzhou-24 mission. He will be China's first astronaut to complete a one year in orbit stay, experiencing the full cycle of "seasons" aboard the Tiangong. The three astronauts of Shenzhou-24 will meet with Chinese and international journalists at the Wentian Pavilion of the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in Gansu Province, on Tuesday.

item.title: With its own climate governance arrears unpaid, how can Western media expect China to 'pick up the tab'?: Global Times editorial
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-23 22:52:00
COP31 President Murat Kurum (center) leaves a closing plenary session at the COP31 UN Climate Summit in Antalya, Turkey, on November 22, 2026. The 31st COP31 failed to reach a consensus on the Antalya Pact. Photo: VCG When negotiations break down, China is blamed for being "unwilling to take the lead"; yet when China provides green production capacity to the world, some media outlets sensationalize the "China shock" and "overcapacity" narratives. Either way, China is always made to take the blame. If the West truly welcomes greater contributions from China to global emissions reduction, it should first work to remove the various discriminatory policies targeting China's new energy exports. The repeatedly extended United Nations (UN) Climate Change Conference (COP31), in Antalya, Turkey, ended in a breakdown of negotiations. This marks the first time since 2009 that a UN climate conference has "ended without agreement," and it was also the longest-running session since the first conference in 1995. Before the conference closed, Reuters, citing the US government's absence, questioned why China was unwilling to be the world's next climate leader. In this framing, obligations developed countries should honor are twisted as something they can sit back and wait for China to "pick up the tab" - an absurd inversion of accountability. The primary reason for the breakdown in negotiations at this conference was that the final draft failed to include clear provisions regarding the transition away from fossil fuels. Parties such as the European Union (EU) refused to accept the text because the final draft made no mention of fossil fuels. With nearly 200 parties harboring divergent priorities, reaching a consensus inherently requires all sides to make compromises on specific provisions. Attributing the failure of the negotiations to China's "unwillingness to take the lead" not only overlooks the concessions China made to seek consensus but also fails to explain the differences among parties regarding the transition away from fossil fuels. Not to mention that developed countries represented by Europe have come under heavy criticism during the negotiations for obstructing progress on multiple fronts, including adaptation finance and just transition. The EU's climate chief even publicly stated before the meeting that talks on "new climate finance commitments" were "dead in the water," ruling out any new commitments to large-scale climate pledges. This stance sparked dissatisfaction among many countries. Some European media outlets chose to overlook this. Instead, by citing the so-called "reluctance of China to take the lead," they sought to discredit China's efforts in addressing climate change. One cannot help but wonder whether this move is intended to evade their own historical responsibilities. Reaching a consensus requires the joint efforts of all nations, and there has long been a clear division of responsibilities regarding taking the lead in emissions reductions and providing funding. The Paris Agreement reaffirmed the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities, clearly stipulating that developed countries should continue to take the lead in reducing emissions and have an obligation to provide financial assistance for mitigation and adaptation measures in developing countries. Insufficient funding will delay climate adaptation projects - such as flood control and water supply - and weaken developing countries' ability to withstand climate disasters. Leveling such accusations against China does not absolve developed countries of their financial obligations. For a transition affordable to all nations, adequate financial support must be in place, and emission reduction technologies must also be accessible at manageable costs. China's push in Antalya to discuss trade barriers was aimed precisely at this latter point. Ahead of the conference, the EU urged major emitters, including China, to step up their emission reductions, yet electric vehicles (EVs) originating in China still face additional anti-subsidy duties when entering the EU market. This contradictory approach is also reflected in the biases of Western narratives. When negotiations break down, China is blamed for being "unwilling to take the lead"; yet when China provides green production capacity to the world, the media sensationalizes the "China shock" and "overcapacity." Either way, China is always made to take the blame. If the West truly welcomes greater contributions from China to global emissions reduction, it should first work to remove the various discriminatory policies targeting China's new energy exports. According to estimates by the International Energy Agency (IEA), even when emissions from both vehicle manufacturing and use are taken into account, a medium-sized battery-electric vehicle still produces fewer emissions on average than a comparable gasoline-powered vehicle. The same applies to solar photovoltaics. As solar panels become cheaper, projects previously shelved due to high costs become economically viable, allowing local communities to replace coal- or gas-fired power with solar energy sooner. The emissions reductions occur in the countries where these products are used, and helping accelerate that transition is precisely China's contribution. Imposing tariffs on Chinese products that could help reduce domestic emissions, while simultaneously urging China to do more to combat climate change, will only make it harder for those countries to achieve their own emissions reduction targets. China's enormous contributions to global climate governance in recent years are evident to all. According to IEA estimates that account for emissions from electricity generation and fuel supply, the stock of EVs was responsible for avoiding net emissions of 190 Mt CO2‑equivalent (CO2-eq) in 2025 compared with equivalent gasoline-powered vehicles, with more than half of those reductions attributable to EV deployment in China. Last year, China provided developing countries with $132 billion in clean technologies and investment, nearly matching the total climate finance provided by all developed nations in 2024. According to estimates by overseas research institutions, this year alone, China's exports of clean energy equipment are expected to reduce emissions overseas by approximately 450 million metric tons of carbon dioxide. These achievements are "unparalleled globally." During this year's climate conference, the Chinese delegation participated in negotiations and consultations on 165 agenda items and held more than 50 bilateral meetings at the ministerial level, making tremendous efforts to encourage all parties to work toward common ground. Ahead of the next round of negotiations, developed countries should translate their financial commitments into funding for concrete projects, continue to take the lead in reducing emissions at home, and give green products a fair opportunity to compete. China has already transformed many once-expensive low-carbon technologies into affordable products accessible to more countries and households, and has demonstrated that a development pathway combining wind and solar power, energy storage, and EVs is both technically and economically viable, representing one of its greatest contributions to the global low-carbon transition. It is abundantly clear that addressing climate change requires a collective effort by countries around the world.

item.title: GT Voice: South Korea's vehicle sector can steer clear of China deficit debate
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-23 22:37:00
An NEV manufacturing line in Southwest China's Chongqing Municipality Photo: VCG South Korea's vehicle trade deficit with China reached a record $4.231 billion in the first 10 months of this year, 4.5 times the full-year figure for 2023, according to The Chosun Daily. China's growing competitiveness in auto manufacturing is increasingly being felt in the South Korean market, but that does not mean that the two countries' economic interests are necessarily at odds. However, a more defensive view has emerged in South Korea. The Chosun Daily reported growing concerns that Chinese electric vehicles (EVs) could account for more than 50 percent of sales in South Korea next year, prompting the automotive industry to "urgently demand countermeasures." Yet there is more to this issue than competition alone. A different picture emerges from a business event in Changchun, Northeast China's Jilin Province in May. The Seoul Economic Daily reported that the Korea Trade-Investment Promotion Agency organized an export consultation as part of stepped-up efforts to help South Korean auto parts makers tap opportunities in China, where sales of eco-friendly vehicles are growing. China is an important export market for South Korean auto parts. Although China's domestic supply chain is well established, the South Korean industry sees scope to expand exports in specialized fields such as automotive electronics, software and lightweight materials. This points to another dimension of the trade that bilateral statistics rarely capture. South Korean-made components can enter China's automotive supply chains, become part of vehicles assembled by Chinese manufacturers and serve consumers in China and overseas. Some of those vehicles may even be exported back to South Korea. In trade statistics, the components are recorded as South Korean exports to China, while the finished vehicles are counted as Chinese exports to South Korea, adding to South Korea's recorded automotive trade deficit with China. Seen in this light, making the trade deficit the focus of the debate misses the point. The vehicle industries of the two neighboring countries are already intertwined through complementary strengths. As supply chains grow more complex, the distinction between trade surpluses and deficits becomes less meaningful, with companies on both sides contributing to production and benefiting from one another's markets. What South Korea's auto industry urgently needs is not a response to its trade deficit with China, let alone a demand for countermeasures. It is to strengthen its own competitiveness, move up the value chain and find new sources of growth. Put simply, the industry should be moving forward, not stopping to defend itself against China. South Korea is no newcomer to the global vehicle industry. It has established internationally recognized brands and a substantial manufacturing base. The industry put in a strong performance in October, after a period of month-to-month fluctuations. Its automobile exports rose 18.1 percent year-on-year to $6.55 billion in October, while domestic production increased 25.8 percent to 381,000 units. Vehicles are among South Korea's most important export products. The country's auto industry has long been closely connected to international markets, with overseas sales playing an important part in its development. Its next phase of growth will depend on strengthening its position in established markets while making further inroads into emerging ones. Expanding its global reach will be essential to sustaining the industry's growth. Competition between the Chinese and South Korean auto industries is real, but it is only part of the picture. There is also scope for cooperation, particularly across the parts supply chain. Such cooperation can benefit both sides, helping South Korean suppliers strengthen their competitiveness and reach customers in third-party markets. As the global auto industry moves toward electrification, the opportunities extend well beyond the two countries' bilateral trade. Emerging markets in particular offer considerable room for growth as more countries embark on the transition to electric mobility. South Korea's auto industry has little to gain from being caught up in debates over whether its trade with China is in surplus or deficit. What matters more is making better use of cooperation in regional supply chains to strengthen its own capabilities, further expand its presence in international markets and help drive the transition to electric mobility in emerging economies.
